name: Phendimetrazine

lead: Phendimetrazine (Bontril) is an older prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite, so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

About 30 percent of an oral dose is converted in the body to phenmetrazine, which releases norepinephrine and dopamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher. Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse.

paras: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period with a reduced-calorie diet. It is mentioned alongside other older prescription appetite suppressants.

The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, agitation and other stimulant effects, and cites a link between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension. Safe use in pregnancy is not established. It is Schedule III in the US.

angle.text: Phendimetrazine is a stimulant that suppresses appetite, so calorie intake falls and weight comes down. It is an older prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

lead: Phendimetrazine (brand names include Bontril) is a prescription stimulant of the morpholine class used as an appetite suppressant. By reducing hunger while someone follows a calorie-restricted plan, it is used to help lower body weight and body fat, which changes how the face and body look. The US label indicates it as a short-term adjunct, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted regimen in patients with a body mass index of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet or exercise alone. [1][2]

It acts largely as a prodrug: Wikipedia states roughly 30% of an oral dose is converted to phenmetrazine, a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent. [2] It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US. [2] Phenmetrazine itself was introduced in Europe in the 1950s as the trade product Preludin, and phendimetrazine was developed from the same Boehringer Ingelheim chemistry. [2][3]

Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse; reviews list phendimetrazine alongside phentermine, diethylpropion and benzphetamine as sympathomimetic drugs approved only for short-term use. [4][5] In bodybuilding and physique-focused forums it appears as one of several prescription options people ask about when cutting body fat. [6]
infobox: Bontril, Bontril PDM, Adipost, Statobex and others [2]

paras: The appearance rationale is indirect: a stimulant that blunts appetite makes it easier for some people to stay in a calorie deficit, and sustained fat loss changes facial fullness and body composition. In physique communities, people preparing for a cut sometimes ask about prescribed appetite suppressants such as Bontril as an alternative to other tools. [6] Prescribing information does not describe any cosmetic indication, and Grokipedia notes the drug is not intended for cosmetic purposes. [7]

The label describes use for exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct in patients with BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise. [1] Grokipedia adds that use beyond about 12 weeks is not established and that tolerance limits long-term effect; it also reports average additional weight loss of 3 to 5 kg over 12 weeks in controlled trials of sympathomimetic agents, a figure not verified against primary trial reports. [7]

Drug-class reviews describe the older sympathomimetic anorectics as agents approved for periods of 12 weeks or less, in contrast with newer medicines approved for longer-term use. [5][8] A 2016 primary-care review groups phendimetrazine among stimulant options and notes that, because of misuse potential, many obesity medications are controlled substances. [9]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia, elevated blood pressure and ischemic events, and central nervous system effects including overstimulation, restlessness, insomnia, agitation, tremor, headache and psychotic state. [1] It warns against combination with other anorectics, including over-the-counter and herbal products, and cites a case-control study linking anorectic use longer than three months to a 23-fold increase in pulmonary hypertension risk. [1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics, but the label says no case had been reported with phendimetrazine alone. [1] Safe use in pregnancy has not been established (Pregnancy Category C). [1]
A 2005 safety review of obesity drugs recounts the history of withdrawn anorectics and then reviews the safety of the agents then available, including phendimetrazine. [10]

Phendimetrazine is described as largely inactive itself, with activity coming from conversion to phenmetrazine; Wikipedia says this produces steadier exposure and that the compound is regarded as having lower abuse potential than phenmetrazine. [2] Adding an N-methyl group to phenmetrazine yields phendimetrazine, which Wikipedia describes as an amphetamine congener acting as a norepinephrine-dopamine releasing agent after conversion. [2] A 2002 laboratory study examined its interaction and that of its metabolites with monoamine transporters in rat brain. [11]

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 19 to 24 hours, with hepatic metabolism and urinary excretion, while Grokipedia reports a shorter figure of about 3.7 hours for the parent drug; the sources differ. [2][7] Sustained-action formulations were studied as early as the 1960s and 1970s, including a 1968 controlled trial of sustained-action phendimetrazine in obesity and a 1975 study of availability from sustained and non-sustained formulations. [12][13]

Phendimetrazine is 3,4-dimethyl-2-phenylmorpholine (also called mephenmetrazine) and belongs to the phenylmorpholine class, structurally related to amphetamines. [2] It is supplied as the tartrate salt. [7]

Phenmetrazine was first patented by Boehringer Ingelheim in 1952 and entered clinical use in Europe in 1954 as an appetite suppressant; Wikipedia reports that its misuse led to withdrawal from many markets, and that phendimetrazine, its prodrug, largely replaced it. [3] A US patent covering the synthesis route of phendimetrazine, naming Werner Heel and Karl Zeile and assigned to C. H. Boehringer Sohn, dates to 1961. [2] Prescription anti-obesity drug use in the US was later tracked by national databases from 1991 to 2011, a period in which phentermine dominated and other short-term agents were prescribed less often. [14]

Phendimetrazine is Schedule III in the US, Schedule IV in Canada, Class B2 in Brazil, and is listed under Schedule III of the international Convention on Psychotropic Substances. [2] Germany restricts it to authorised trade and does not allow prescription. [2] A 2018 analysis examined US health-policy and insurance coverage of FDA-approved obesity drugs, and a 2013 study examined prescribing of anti-obesity drugs in the US. [15][14] A survey of physician obesity specialists found that nearly all prescribed medications and that phentermine was the one all recommended. [16]
Phendimetrazine appears by name in banned-stimulant lists that T Nation forum members have posted when discussing supplements and drug testing for athletes. [17][18]

Older controlled trials examined sustained-action phendimetrazine in obesity and its effect on plasma lipids in the 1960s and 1970s. [12][19] Reviews of obesity pharmacotherapy summarise this older evidence on noradrenergic anorectics, including phendimetrazine. [4][20][5] No studies found of phendimetrazine for appearance-related or cosmetic goals.

More recent human trials have studied phendimetrazine for a different purpose. A controlled study in nine cocaine-dependent volunteers evaluated its abuse potential, and a randomized trial examined how phendimetrazine maintenance influenced the effects of intranasal cocaine. [21][22] Registered US trials of these designs enrolled 11 and 30 participants. [23][24] These are not studies of weight loss. In animals, phendimetrazine reduced choice of cocaine over food in rhesus monkeys over 14 days of treatment, and rats showed cocaine-like discriminative effects. [25][26]

lore.intro: Phendimetrazine is mentioned occasionally on bodybuilding forums as a prescribed appetite suppressant for cutting, and appears in banned-substance lists posted for athletes. [6][17]

claims.claim: A prescribed appetite suppressant like Bontril helps people cut body fat.
Phendimetrazine is detectable in or banned by sports testing.
